newsitem.title: FRANCE: French far-right stages racially-charged march.
newsitem.headline: French far-right stages racially-charged march.

text.p: French extreme-right politician Jean-Marie Le Pen, ignoring charges of racism, led supporters on a tightly-policed march on Saturday to mourn a white teenager allegedly killed by a youth of Arab origin.

"France for the French", "Le Pen for president", the protesters shouted as they walked through the Mediterranean port of Marseille, guarded by hundreds of police. Counter-protesters by the route booed and denounced the marchers as racists.

Police reckoned 2,000 people attended Le Pen's rally for 14-year-old Nicolas Bourgat, stabbed to death on Tuesday. Organisers estimated 4,000 took part, with banners including "Protect our children" and "Immigration equals insecurity".
Le Pen, already at the centre of a furore this week after he openly espoused a doctrine of racial inequality, said he was staging the march "to show respect for an assassinated fellow citizen".
Nicolas' father, a local doctor, was among many who pleaded against Le Pen's march, saying he did not want his son's death hijacked for political ends.

Nicolas was to be buried in Marseille at 2.30 (1230 GMT). Marseille mayor Jean-Claude Gaudin, who is also Urban Affairs Minister, appealed for calm and dignity ordered church bells to ring at 2.30 to signal five minutes' silence.
Four anti-National Front women went to the front of the rally brandishing a poster saying "Front Hatred". They were led away by police.
A 15-year-old French boy of North African origin, named only as Ktab, was placed under investigation on suspicion of murder on Friday. He is being held in preventive detention.
Meanwhile, Justice Minister Jacques Toubon said a draft bill tightening laws against racism could be passed to parliament next month.

The planned laws would make even indirect provocations to discrimination, hatred or violence a crime, he told the daily Liberation. And Toubon said they would also stiffen sentences for racist crimes.

Le Pen has been under fire for saying that racial inequality was a "fact" and that some civilisations, like the French, are superior. One Socialist opposition politician to call this week for the National Front to be outlawed.

Toubon told the daily Liberation that he found Le Pen's remarks "totally reprehensible" but said he could not be prosecuted under existing laws which he said can only sanction direct provocations for racial hatred.
On Friday, French President Jacques Chirac visited the former Nazi extermination camp at Auschwitz during a visit to Poland and called for vigilance against possible future anti-Semitism.

France's political establishment is perplexed as to how to reverse the rise of Le Pen, who won 15 percent in last year's presidential election by blaming immigration for unemployment, crime and insecurity and calling for three million immigrants to be sent home.
The National Front is vying with Juppe's Gaullist RPR party and the opposition Communists for the working-class vote in the run-up to parliamentary elections in 1998.
